articles.title: Regret is rare among transgender youth who began hormone therapy, according to largest study of its kind
articles.summary: Most people who began hormone therapy as teenagers at a U.S. gender clinic and answered a follow-up survey said starting treatment had been the right decision, according to a cohort study published in JAMA Pediatrics. Even among former patients who eventually stopped taking hormones, more than four out of five still reported that starting treatment […]

articles.title: Psychedelics show anti-inflammatory effects in sick animals but not healthy ones, meta-analysis finds
articles.summary: Psychedelics consistently reduced inflammatory markers in lab and animal studies where inflammation had been induced, but not in healthy animals. A review of 61 studies found human evidence too limited to draw conclusions.

articles.title: Neuroscientists just found a hidden “fingerprint” in human memory
articles.summary: Electrical rhythms that sweep across the brain’s surface don’t just move in straight lines. Recordings from neurosurgical patients show they also form spirals and expanding or contracting rings that shift as people store and recall memories.

articles.title: New study finds vulnerable narcissism is linked to harsher judgments of police stops, even polite ones
articles.summary: Two drivers can experience the same traffic stop very differently. A new experiment suggests that people higher in vulnerable narcissism rate police stops less favorably, even when the officer is polite and fair.

articles.title: Zugwise: Domain-Aware Game Reconstruction for Digitizing Handwritten Chess Scoresheets
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digitizing handwritten chess scoresheets has been studied as a handwriting-recognition problem: read the move in each box and check that it is legal. This framing misses the errors that matter most. A misread that yields an illegal move is loud. articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adversarial Machine Learning research is currently centered on the search for the epsilon-ball: minimal perturbations designed to fool models while remaining imperceptible to humans. articles.title: StructRL: Model-Free Reinforcement Learning with Replay Graphs
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: StructRL turns the experience collected during reinforcement learning into an explicit replay graph. articles.title: Mind-wandering preserves word-level coupling while disrupting comprehension
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Readers can move their eyes through a page but retain little of its meaning when their minds wander. We tested whether word properties still guide their eyes during these lapses. We analyzed public eye-tracking and electroencephalography (EEG) data from 44 adults who read articles. articles.title: Tracking the connection between bipolar disorder and sexual distress
articles.summary: A new six-month study tracks how depressive symptoms and daily mood swings impact sexual desire and frustration in people newly diagnosed with bipolar disorder. The research highlights the need to address sexual health between major mood episodes.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work
